name: Where AI Falls Short
title: Where AI Falls Short
answer: AI fails in six predictable ways: it invents facts, gives inconsistent answers, carries bias, does not know individual students, cannot be held responsible, and may store what users type. Knowing these failures in advance is most of what it takes to use AI safely, and every use needs a plan for catching mistakes. The failures do not mean schools should avoid AI, but they do mean no output should be trusted without a person checking it.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: This idea sets out the six predictable ways generative AI falls short so that schools can plan for them rather than be surprised by them. The first is invention, where the tool makes up a quote, statistic, book title, or court case and states it as confidently as a true fact, and no tool on the market has eliminated these errors. The second is inconsistency, where the same tool gives different answers on different runs. The third is bias, since AI learns from data made by people, including their blind spots. The remaining failures are that AI does not know your students, cannot be held responsible when something goes wrong, and in some free tools stores what users type. The problem it solves is that knowing these failure modes ahead of time is most of what safe use requires.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the six failures translate into concrete habits. Anything that will be shared with families, graded, or used to make a decision needs a person to check it against a real source, because invention cannot be eliminated by any tool. A tool that cannot give the same answer twice should not be scoring a teacher's job performance, so inconsistent outputs are kept away from evaluation. Teachers remain the ones who know that a boy stopped turning in homework after his grandmother died, or that a girl reads well above grade level but freezes on timed tests, and no amount of data replaces that knowledge. In the tutoring study described earlier, human tutors caught AI suggestions that were too advanced or not right for the grade level. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with named studies and findings. One 2026 study had eight AI systems rate 12 videos of elementary classrooms and compared the ratings with those of certified human observers; the AI scores changed from one run to the next, matched the experts only moderately at best, and leaned on what teachers said out loud rather than what was happening in the room (Melo et al., 2026). A widely cited study found that tools built to detect AI writing often flagged essays by writers whose first language is not English as machine written when they were not (Liang et al., 2023). One test company built detectors that showed no such bias on its own adult test data, but a school cannot assume the tool it buys behaves that way (Jiang et al., 2024). The text also states that no tool on the market has eliminated invention errors.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are the six failures themselves, and the decisions that stay with a person follow from them. A person must check anything shared with families, graded, or used for a decision against a real source, because invention cannot be trusted. A person must keep inconsistent tools away from judging teacher performance, since a tool that cannot repeat its answer should not score a teacher's job. A person must watch for bias, because a student learning English could be accused of cheating for writing simply, and a school cannot assume the tool it buys is free of the bias found in other detectors. A person must supply the knowledge of students that AI lacks, and a person must be the one who answers for a wrong grade or an upset family, because software cannot. Finally, a person must decide what is safe to type, since some free AI tools store what users type and use it to improve their products, and typing a student's name, disability, or discipline record into the wrong tool can break federal and state privacy law.
